nodes.label: The distance between two points
nodes.description: Find the distance between two points using the distance rule: on the x-axis |x2−x1|, on the y-axis |y2−y1|, and in general MN = √((x2−x1)²+(y2−y1)²) via the Pythagorean theorem; distance of M(x1,y1) from the origin O = √(x1²+y1²).

nodes.label: Applying the distance rule to geometric figures
nodes.description: Use the distance rule to prove properties of figures: identify squares/rhombi/rectangles by side and diagonal lengths, right triangles by the converse of the Pythagorean theorem, points on a circle equidistant from its center, and collinear points where AB + BC = AC.

nodes.label: Coordinates of the midpoint of a segment
nodes.description: Find the two coordinates of the midpoint of a line segment with ends (x1,y1), (x2,y2): M((x1+x2)/2, (y1+y2)/2), including segments parallel to the axes.

nodes.label: Using the midpoint rule
nodes.description: Use the midpoint rule in reverse to find an unknown endpoint given the midpoint, and apply it to parallelograms: the diagonals bisect each other, so their intersection point is the midpoint of both diagonals.

nodes.label: The slope of a straight line
nodes.description: Compute the slope through two points m = (y2−y1)/(x2−x1); slope = tan E where E is the positive angle the line makes with the positive direction of the x-axis; sign of the slope by angle type (acute → m>0, obtuse → m<0, zero → m=0, right → undefined).

nodes.label: Slopes of parallel straight lines
nodes.description: If L1 ∥ L2 then m1 = m2 and vice versa; lines parallel to the x-axis have slope 0, lines parallel to the y-axis have equal x-coordinates (undefined slope).

nodes.label: Slopes of perpendicular straight lines
nodes.description: If L1 ⊥ L2 then m1 × m2 = −1 and vice versa; use the product rule to find perpendicular slopes and to prove a triangle is right-angled at a vertex.

nodes.label: The equation y = mx + b: slope and y-intercept
nodes.description: Read the slope m (coefficient of x) and the y-intercept b from y = mx + b; convert ax + by + c = 0 (b ≠ 0) to that form, where m = −a/b = −(coefficient of x)/(coefficient of y).

nodes.label: Finding the equation of a straight line
nodes.description: Write the equation of a line given its slope and a point on it (substitute to find c in y = mx + c), including lines parallel or perpendicular to a given line and lines bisecting a given segment (through its midpoint).

questions.stem: The two points $A(2, 0)$ and $B(6, 0)$ are both located on the x-axis. The length of $\overline{AB} =$ … unit length.
solution: The two points are both located on the x-axis, so the distance is the absolute difference of the x-coordinates: $AB = |x_2 - x_1|$.
So $AB = 4$ unit length.
questions.source_note: Original question; distance on the x-axis, cf. case 1 A(3,0), B(-1,0), p.58

questions.stem: Find the length of $\overline{CD}$ where $C(0, -2)$ and $D(0, 3)$.
solution: The two points are both located on the y-axis (both have $x = 0$), so $CD = |y_2 - y_1|$.
So $CD = 5$ unit length.
questions.source_note: Original question; distance on the y-axis, cf. case 2 C(0,-3), D(0,-1), p.58

questions.stem: Find the distance between the two points $M(1, 2)$ and $N(4, 6)$.
solution: The distance between two points $(x_1, y_1)$, $(x_2, y_2) = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}$.
$MN = 5$ unit length.
questions.source_note: Original variant of the M(3,2), N(7,5) worked case (same 3-4-5 skeleton), pp.58-59

questions.stem: The distance of the point $M(6, 8)$ from the origin point $O(0, 0)$ equals … unit length.
solution: The distance of a point $M(x_1, y_1)$ from the origin $O(0, 0)$ is $OM = \sqrt{x_1^2 + y_1^2}$ (Remark, Lesson 5-1).
$OM = 10$ unit length — note that $100$ forgets the square root and $14$ just adds the coordinates.
questions.source_note: Original question; distance from the origin remark, p.59

questions.stem: If the distance between the two points $A(3, y)$ and $B(6, 4)$ is $5$ unit length, and $y > 0$, find the value of $y$.
solution: Apply the distance rule: $AB = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}$, so $\sqrt{(6-3)^2 + (4-y)^2} = 5$.
Square both sides: $9 + (4 - y)^2 = 25$, so $(4 - y)^2 = 16$.
Then $4 - y = 4$ or $4 - y = -4$, giving $y = 0$ or $y = 8$.
Since $y > 0$, we take $y = 8$.
questions.source_note: Original question; reverse use of the distance rule, p.59

questions.stem: The triangle whose vertices are $A(1, 1)$, $B(4, 1)$ and $C(4, 5)$ is right-angled at …

choices.text: no vertex — it is not right-angled

solution: By the converse of the Pythagorean theorem, the angle opposite to $\overline{AC}$ is right, so the triangle is right-angled at $B$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of Example 2 (right triangle by converse of Pythagoras, new vertices), p.60

questions.stem: Find the surface area of the triangle whose vertices are $A(1, 1)$, $B(4, 1)$ and $C(4, 5)$, in square units.
solution: From the distance rule: $AB = \sqrt{(4-1)^2 + (1-1)^2} = 3$ and $BC = \sqrt{(4-4)^2 + (5-1)^2} = 4$.
$(AB)^2 + (BC)^2 = 9 + 16 = 25 = (AC)^2$, so the triangle is right-angled at $B$ (converse of the Pythagorean theorem).
Area $= \frac{1}{2} \times AB \times BC = \frac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 4 = 6$ square units.
questions.source_note: Original question; surface area of a right triangle as in Example 2, p.60

questions.stem: A circle has center $O(0, 0)$ and passes through the point $(3, 4)$. Which of the following points does NOT lie on this circle?
solution: The radius is the distance from the center to $(3, 4)$: $r = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5$.
A point lies on the circle when its distance from the center equals $5$: $(5,0) \to \sqrt{25} = 5$ ✓; $(0,-5) \to \sqrt{25} = 5$ ✓; $(-4,3) \to \sqrt{16+9} = 5$ ✓.
$(4, 4) \to \sqrt{4^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{32} \neq 5$, so $(4, 4)$ does not lie on the circle.
questions.source_note: Original variant of Example 3 (points equidistant from a circle's center), p.60

questions.stem: If the four points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ have all four sides equal in length AND the two diagonals equal in length, then the figure $ABCD$ is a …

choices.text: rhombus that is not a square
rectangle that is not a square

solution: Equal sides make the figure a rhombus (Drill, Lesson 5-1).
If in addition the two diagonals are equal in length, the rhombus is a square.
This is exactly the check used in Example 1: sides all $\sqrt{41}$ and diagonals both $\sqrt{82}$ prove a square.
questions.source_note: Original question; conditions drill + Example 1 square check, pp.59-60

questions.stem: For the points $A(0, 0)$, $B(3, 4)$ and $C(6, 8)$: $AB = 5$, $BC = 5$ and $AC = 10$. Since $AB + BC = AC$, the three points are …

choices.text: located on a circle whose center is $B$

solution: Check the distances with the rule: $AB = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$, $BC = \sqrt{(6-3)^2 + (8-4)^2} = 5$, $AC = \sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$.
When the sum of two distances equals the third, the middle point lies on the segment joining the other two: the points $A$, $B$ and $C$ are collinear — they cannot form a triangle at all.
questions.source_note: Original variant of the collinearity drill (A(4,3), B(1,1), C(-5,-3) → clean 3-4-5 multiples), p.61

questions.stem: The coordinates of point $C$, the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$ where $A(2, 6)$ and $B(4, 0)$, are …
solution: The midpoint of the segment with ends $(x_1, y_1)$, $(x_2, y_2)$ is $M\left(\dfrac{x_1 + x_2}{2}, \dfrac{y_1 + y_2}{2}\right)$.
$C\left(\dfrac{2 + 4}{2}, \dfrac{6 + 0}{2}\right) = C\left(\dfrac{6}{2}, \dfrac{6}{2}\right)$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of Drill case 1 A(2,4), B(6,0) (new numbers), p.63

questions.stem: Find the x-coordinate of the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$ where $A(-3, 5)$ and $B(7, 1)$.
solution: The x-coordinate of the midpoint is $x = \dfrac{x_1 + x_2}{2}$.
(The full midpoint is $(2, 3)$, since $y = \dfrac{5 + 1}{2} = 3$.)
questions.source_note: Original question; midpoint rule, p.63

questions.stem: The segment with the two ends $A(-4, -1)$ and $B(-4, -7)$ is parallel to the y-axis. The coordinates of its midpoint are …
solution: Both ends have $x = -4$, so the segment is parallel to the y-axis and its midpoint keeps $x = -4$.
So the midpoint is $(-4, -4)$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of the Second case A(-2,-5), B(-2,-1) (segment parallel to y-axis), p.62

questions.stem: The origin point $O(0, 0)$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$ where $A(a, 3)$ and $B(5, b)$. Find the value of $a + b$.
solution: Apply the midpoint rule to each coordinate: $\dfrac{a + 5}{2} = 0$ and $\dfrac{3 + b}{2} = 0$.
From the first: $a + 5 = 0$, so $a = -5$.
From the second: $3 + b = 0$, so $b = -3$.
Therefore $a + b = -5 + (-3) = -8$.
questions.source_note: Original question; midpoint rule solved backwards for both coordinates, p.63

questions.stem: If $M(3, k)$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$ where $A(1, 2)$ and $B(5, 6)$, find the value of $k$.
solution: The midpoint of $\overline{AB}$ is $\left(\dfrac{1 + 5}{2}, \dfrac{2 + 6}{2}\right) = (3, 4)$.
Comparing with $M(3, k)$: $k = 4$.
questions.source_note: Original question; midpoint rule with one unknown coordinate, p.63

questions.stem: If $C(2, 1)$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$ where $A(-1, 3)$, then the coordinates of point $B$ are …
solution: Consider $B(x_2, y_2)$. Since $C$ is the midpoint: $x = \dfrac{x_1 + x_2}{2}$ and $y = \dfrac{y_1 + y_2}{2}$.
Therefore $B(5, -1)$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of Example 1 (find the endpoint from the midpoint), p.63

questions.stem: $C(0, 2)$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$ where $A(4, -2)$. Find the y-coordinate of point $B$.
solution: Consider $B(x_2, y_2)$; the midpoint rule gives $y = \dfrac{y_1 + y_2}{2}$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of Example 1 (endpoint from midpoint, new numbers), p.63

questions.stem: $ABCD$ is a parallelogram where $A(1, 2)$, $B(4, 3)$ and $C(5, 6)$. The coordinates of point $D$ are …
solution: In a parallelogram the two diagonals bisect each other, so the intersection point $M$ is the midpoint of both $\overline{AC}$ and $\overline{BD}$.
$M$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AC}$: $M\left(\dfrac{1+5}{2}, \dfrac{2+6}{2}\right) = M(3, 4)$.
$M$ is also the midpoint of $\overline{BD}$ with $D(x_1, y_1)$: $3 = \dfrac{4 + x_1}{2}$ gives $x_1 = 2$, and $4 = \dfrac{3 + y_1}{2}$ gives $y_1 = 5$.
Therefore $D(2, 5)$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of Example 2 (parallelogram A(3,2), B(4,-5), C(0,-3) → D via diagonals), p.64

questions.stem: In the parallelogram $ABCD$, the point at which the two diagonals intersect is …

choices.text: the midpoint of each of the two diagonals $\overline{AC}$ and $\overline{BD}$

solution: In a parallelogram, the two diagonals bisect each other.
So their intersection point $M$ is the midpoint of the diagonal $\overline{AC}$ and at the same time the midpoint of the diagonal $\overline{BD}$ — this is the property used to find a missing vertex.
questions.source_note: Original question; property behind Example 2, p.64

questions.stem: $ABCD$ is a parallelogram where $A(2, -1)$ and $C(6, 3)$. If $M$ is the point of intersection of its two diagonals, find the sum of the two coordinates of $M$.
solution: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so $M$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AC}$.
Sum of the coordinates $= 4 + 1 = 5$.
questions.source_note: Original question; diagonal intersection as a midpoint, p.64

questions.stem: Find the slope of the straight line passing through the two points $(1, 2)$ and $(3, 6)$.
solution: The slope of the straight line passing through $(x_1, y_1)$, $(x_2, y_2)$ equals $\dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$.
questions.source_note: Original question; slope rule, cf. Think and Discuss First (3,1), (4,2), p.65

questions.stem: If a straight line makes an ACUTE positive angle with the positive direction of the x-axis, then its slope is …
solution: From the table of Lesson 5-3: when the positive angle the line makes with the positive direction of the x-axis is acute, the slope is larger than zero.
(Obtuse angle → slope smaller than zero; zero angle → slope equal to zero; right angle → slope unidentified.)
questions.source_note: Original question; angle-type/slope-sign table, p.65

questions.stem: The slope of the straight line passing through the two points $(2, -1)$ and $(2, 3)$ is …
solution: $m = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} = \dfrac{3 - (-1)}{2 - 2} = \dfrac{4}{0}$, and division by zero is undefined.
The two points have the same x-coordinate, so the line is vertical: it makes a right angle with the positive direction of the x-axis, and its slope is unidentified.
questions.source_note: Original variant of Think and Discuss Fourth (2,-1), (2,3) — same vertical-line case, p.65

questions.stem: Find the slope of the straight line that makes a positive angle of measure $45°$ with the positive direction of the x-axis.
solution: The slope of a straight line $= \tan E$, where $E$ is the positive angle the line makes with the positive direction of the x-axis.
questions.source_note: Original question; slope = tan E, cf. Drill 1B, p.66

questions.stem: If the slope of the straight line passing through the two points $(3, k)$ and $(5, 7)$ equals $2$, find the value of $k$.
solution: Apply the slope rule: $m = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} = \dfrac{7 - k}{5 - 3} = \dfrac{7 - k}{2}$.
questions.source_note: Original question; slope rule with an unknown coordinate, p.65

questions.stem: If $L_1 \parallel L_2$ and their slopes are $m_1$, $m_2$, then …
solution: If two lines are parallel, then their slopes are equal, and vice versa (Lesson 5-3).
So $L_1 \parallel L_2 \Rightarrow m_1 = m_2$ — the two lines make equal positive angles with the positive direction of the x-axis, and $\tan E_1 = \tan E_2$.
questions.source_note: Original question; parallel-slopes rule box, p.67

questions.stem: The straight line passing through the two points $(2, -1)$ and $(6, 3)$ is parallel to the straight line that makes with the positive direction of the x-axis an angle of measure …
solution: The slope of the line through the two points: $m_1 = \dfrac{3 - (-1)}{6 - 2} = \dfrac{4}{4} = 1$.
The slope of the line making angle $E$: $m_2 = \tan E$. Two lines are parallel when $m_1 = m_2$.
$\tan 45° = 1 = m_1$, so the line is parallel to the line making a $45°$ angle.
questions.source_note: Original question; same skeleton as Drill 2 (2,-1), (6,3) parallel to the 45° line, p.68

questions.stem: If the straight line $\overleftrightarrow{AB} \parallel$ the y-axis, where $A(x, 4)$ and $B(2, 9)$, find the value of $x$.
solution: A straight line parallel to the y-axis is vertical: all its points have the same x-coordinate.
questions.source_note: Original variant of Drill 3 (AB ∥ y-axis, A(x,7), B(3,5)), p.68

questions.stem: If the straight line $\overleftrightarrow{CD} \parallel$ the x-axis, where $C(1, -3)$ and $D(6, y)$, find the value of $y$.
solution: A straight line parallel to the x-axis is horizontal: all its points have the same y-coordinate (its slope is $0$).
questions.source_note: Original variant of Drill 4 (CD ∥ x-axis, C(4,2), D(-5,y)), p.68

questions.stem: The straight line passing through $(0, 0)$ and $(2, 4)$ is parallel to the straight line passing through $(1, 1)$ and $(a, 5)$. Find the value of $a$.
solution: Slope of the first line: $m_1 = \dfrac{4 - 0}{2 - 0} = 2$.
The lines are parallel, so $m_2 = m_1 = 2$: $\dfrac{5 - 1}{a - 1} = 2$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of Drill 1 (parallel lines through given point pairs, unknown coordinate), p.68

questions.stem: If $L_1 \perp L_2$ and their slopes are $m_1, m_2 \in \mathbb{R}^*$, then $m_1 \times m_2 =$ …
solution: The product of multiplying the slopes of two perpendicular straight lines $= -1$, and vice versa (Lesson 5-3).
So $L_1 \perp L_2 \Rightarrow m_1 \times m_2 = -1$.
questions.source_note: Original question; perpendicular-slopes rule box, pp.68-69

questions.stem: The slope of the straight line perpendicular to the straight line passing through the two points $(1, 1)$ and $(3, 5)$ equals …
solution: Slope of the given line: $m_1 = \dfrac{5 - 1}{3 - 1} = \dfrac{4}{2} = 2$.
For the perpendicular line: $m_1 \times m_2 = -1$, so $2 \times m_2 = -1$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of the Drill (perpendicular slope to the line through (3,-2), (5,1)), p.69

questions.stem: A straight line of slope $m$ is perpendicular to a straight line of slope $-4$. Find the value of $m$ (as a decimal).
solution: For perpendicular lines: $m_1 \times m_2 = -1$.
questions.source_note: Original question; direct use of m1 × m2 = -1, p.69

questions.stem: The triangle $XYZ$ has vertices $X(1, 4)$, $Y(2, 1)$ and $Z(5, k)$, and it is right-angled at $Y$. Find the value of $k$.
solution: Slope of $\overleftrightarrow{XY}$: $m_1 = \dfrac{1 - 4}{2 - 1} = -3$.
Slope of $\overleftrightarrow{YZ}$: $m_2 = \dfrac{k - 1}{5 - 2} = \dfrac{k - 1}{3}$.
The triangle is right-angled at $Y$, so $\overleftrightarrow{XY} \perp \overleftrightarrow{YZ}$ and $m_1 \times m_2 = -1$: $-3 \times \dfrac{k - 1}{3} = -1$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of Example 2 (right angle at a vertex → slope product −1, new points), p.69

questions.stem: The straight line passing through the two points $(0, 3)$ and $(3, 0)$ is perpendicular to the straight line that makes with the positive direction of the x-axis an angle of measure …
solution: Slope of the first line: $m_1 = \dfrac{0 - 3}{3 - 0} = -1$.
Slope of the line making angle $E$: $m_2 = \tan E$; for $E = 45°$, $m_2 = \tan 45° = 1$.
$m_1 \times m_2 = -1 \times 1 = -1$, so the two straight lines are perpendicular.
questions.source_note: Original variant of Example 1 (line perpendicular to a line given by its angle), p.69

questions.stem: In the equation of the straight line $y = mx + b$, the symbol $b$ denotes …

choices.text: the slope of the straight line
the x-coordinate of any point on the line
the measure of the positive angle with the x-axis

solution: The equation of the straight line with respect to its slope $(m)$ and the y-intercept $(b)$ is $y = mx + b$ (Definition, Lesson 5-4).
$m$ is the slope (the coefficient of $x$) and $b$ is the length of the y-intercept — the part between the origin and the point where the line cuts the y-axis.
questions.source_note: Original question; definition y = mx + b, pp.70-71

questions.stem: Find the slope of the straight line whose equation is $y = 3x - 2$.
solution: The equation is in the formula $y = mx + b$, where $m$ is the slope.
The coefficient of $x$ is $3$, so the slope $= 3$ (and the y-intercept $= -2$).
questions.source_note: Original question; reading m from y = mx + b, p.71

questions.stem: Find the length of the y-intercept of the straight line whose equation is $2x + y - 6 = 0$.
solution: Write the equation in the formula $y = mx + b$: from $2x + y - 6 = 0$ we get $y = -2x + 6$.
The y-intercept is the constant term: $b = 6$.
(Check: at $x = 0$, $y = 6$, so the line cuts the y-axis at $(0, 6)$.)
questions.source_note: Original variant of Example 1 (rearranging ax + by + c = 0 into y = mx + c), p.71

questions.stem: The slope of the straight line whose equation is $2x + 5y - 10 = 0$ equals …
solution: For the equation in the formula $ax + by + c = 0$, $b \neq 0$: the slope $m = \dfrac{-a}{b} = \dfrac{-\text{coefficient of } x}{\text{coefficient of } y}$.
(Or rearrange: $5y = -2x + 10$, so $y = -\dfrac{2}{5}x + 2$ — same slope, y-intercept $2$.)
questions.source_note: Original variant of Example 1 (slope of 3x + 4y − 5 = 0 in two methods, new coefficients), p.71

questions.stem: For the straight line whose equation is $4x - 2y + 6 = 0$: if $m$ is its slope and $b$ is the length of its y-intercept, find the value of $m + b$.
solution: Slope: $m = \dfrac{-a}{b} = \dfrac{-4}{-2} = 2$.
Rearrange to $y = mx + b$: $2y = 4x + 6$, so $y = 2x + 3$, giving the y-intercept $b = 3$.
questions.source_note: Original question; combining m = −a/b with the y-intercept, p.71

questions.stem: The equation of the straight line whose slope is $2$ and whose y-intercept is $5$ is …
solution: Substitute directly in the formula $y = mx + b$ with $m = 2$ and $b = 5$.
The equation is $y = 2x + 5$.
questions.source_note: Original question; writing the equation from m and b, p.71

questions.stem: A straight line of slope $3$ passes through the point $(1, 2)$. If its equation is $y = 3x + c$, find the value of $c$.
solution: The line passes through the point $(1, 2)$, so the point satisfies the equation.
Substitute: $2 = 3 \times 1 + c$.
$c = 2 - 3 = -1$, so the equation is $y = 3x - 1$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of Example 2 (finding c from a point on the line), p.71

questions.stem: The equation of the straight line passing through the point $(0, 4)$ and parallel to the straight line $y = 2x - 1$ is …
solution: Parallel lines have equal slopes, so the required slope $m = 2$.
The line cuts the y-axis at $(0, 4)$, so its y-intercept $b = 4$.
Substitute in $y = mx + b$: the equation is $y = 2x + 4$.
questions.source_note: Original question; equation of a parallel line from m and b, p.71

questions.stem: The equation of the straight line passing through the point $(2, 1)$ and perpendicular to the straight line passing through the two points $(1, 5)$ and $(3, 1)$ is …
solution: Slope of the line through $(1, 5)$ and $(3, 1)$: $m_1 = \dfrac{1 - 5}{3 - 1} = \dfrac{-4}{2} = -2$.
The required line is perpendicular to it, so $m_1 \times m_2 = -1$: $-2 \times m_2 = -1$, giving $m_2 = \dfrac{1}{2}$.
Write $y = \dfrac{1}{2}x + c$; the line passes through $(2, 1)$, so $1 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 + c = 1 + c$, giving $c = 0$.
The equation is $y = \dfrac{1}{2}x$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of Example 2 (line through a point perpendicular to a line through two points), p.71

questions.stem: If $A(0, 1)$, $B(2, 5)$ and $C(4, 3)$, then the equation of the straight line passing through the vertex $A$ and bisecting $\overline{BC}$ is …
solution: The line bisects $\overline{BC}$, so it passes through its midpoint: $\left(\dfrac{2 + 4}{2}, \dfrac{5 + 3}{2}\right) = (3, 4)$.
Slope of the required line through $A(0, 1)$ and $(3, 4)$: $m = \dfrac{4 - 1}{3 - 0} = 1$.
Write $y = mx + c$: the line passes through $A(0, 1)$, so $c = 1$.
The equation is $y = x + 1$.
questions.source_note: Original variant of Example 3 (line through a vertex bisecting the opposite side, new points), p.72
